# Building the rounding check as an agent skill {#sec-workflow-rounding-skill}

::: callout-tip
A useful skill can begin as one visible `SKILL.md`. Add references, scripts, and
templates only when each resource addresses a named weakness in the simpler
version.
:::

During clinical development, the R scripts used for analysis and reporting may
change over time.
The developer must repeat the rounding review from @sec-workflow-rounding-prompt.
The saved response preserves candidate locations, example outputs, explanations, and a
proposed solution, but not a repeatable method: which functions must be
searched, which ties must be tested, how coverage is recorded, or when to stop
before posting an issue. The draft survived the handoff. The ability to
reproduce and evaluate it did not.

@sec-workflow-rounding-prompt established three business rules, defined the scope of
BR-001, and showed how to read an exploratory response as a draft rather than an
answer key. It also named four things a prompt cannot provide: coverage,
repeatability, separation of fixed checks from judgment, and a named human
gate. This chapter turns those gaps into requirements and specifies each stage
of the AI-first SDLC from @sec-ai-first-sdlc.

The [AI-Native SDLC Playbook lesson on skills as institutional
knowledge](https://academy.claude.com/courses/ai-native-sdlc-playbook/skills-as-institutional-knowledge)
describes a skill as a way to make owned, written knowledge operational. This
chapter adapts that idea to Biometrics: BR-001 is the source of truth, the rule
owner controls it, and the skill tells an agent how to apply it during a bounded
review. The skill remains an advisory control. Fixed scripts can produce
repeatable evidence, but a person still approves the rule and classifies the
finding.

The Build stage develops the same proposed skill in two examples. The first
uses only `SKILL.md`, making the trigger, instruction, boundaries, and output
visible in one place. The second keeps that entry point small and adds a rule
reference, fixed scripts, and a report template. Comparing them shows when one
file is enough and when additional resources are justified.

::: {.callout-note title="Maturity: Design pattern"}
The workflow is specified, not distributed. The book contains no installable
skill package, no executable script files, no small test programs, no evidence
files, no automated check on source-code changes, and no scheduled job. The
results quoted at the pinned
`metalite.ae` commit were verified for this book and serve as the answer key for
a future benchmark; they are not evidence that the skill described here has been
built or run. The public issue linked in @sec-workflow-rounding-prompt contains one
Arena.ai response that a person copied to GitHub; it is not output from this
skill or evidence that this workflow was released.

A broader three-rule skill is being developed separately through
[`RConsortium/pharma-skills` issue #208](https://github.com/RConsortium/pharma-skills/issues/208).
That open issue currently defines a benchmark rather than a released rounding
skill, so it does not raise this chapter's maturity level.
:::

The chapter has one main finding: **start with one inspectable instruction, then
add a resource only when the task contract explains what behavior it should
improve.**

- **Problem:** A useful one-off review cannot be repeated reliably when its
  procedure remains in one person's memory.
- **Learning objective:** Build a minimal one-file skill, identify its limits,
  and design a resource-backed version with more reproducible evidence, stated
  coverage, and an accountable human decision.
- **Workflow boundary:** Begin when a reviewer asks whether one folder of R
  files follows the approved tie rule for reported values and row-selection
  decisions; end when a named human classifies each finding.
- **Non-goals:** Build an agent platform, distribute a runnable skill, validate
  statistical methods, replace independent QC, automate human classification,
  cover BR-002 or BR-003 within this chapter, or claim qualification for GxP
  use.
- **Why this is well defined:** One rule, one pinned source folder, observable
  results, explicit boundaries, versioned inputs, and a named decision maker
  keep the task bounded.

## Plan --- Frame the workflow

### Turn the prompt's limits into requirements

The four gaps in @sec-workflow-rounding-prompt are not additional `metalite.ae`
defects. They are limitations of the one-off review, and each one becomes a
workflow requirement:

- replace reviewer memory with a written minimum procedure while leaving room
  for the agent to investigate beyond it;
- report coverage for every run, including rules left unchecked;
- keep fixed, repeatable checks separate from exploratory agent work and
  judgment in the output; and
- name the human who classifies each finding, and stop before any external
  action.

A fifth design need appears when the review is repeated: a previously reviewed
call should not require the same triage on every run. The rule owner may approve
an allowlist entry with its reason and source version. The call remains visible
in coverage, and a source change returns it to review.

The function catalog is a required starting point, not a ceiling. The agent can
follow wrappers, helper functions, or other unexpected code paths, but it must
label candidates found through that exploratory pass separately.

### Canonical artifact: Workflow brief

- **Objective:** Specify a check that finds calls able to round a displayed
  value or a value used in a report decision, tests them against the
  half-away-from-zero rule, and can be performed by a reviewer who did not
  design it.
- **Inputs:** One R source folder at a pinned commit, BR-001 v1.0, the precision
  used by each relevant output, rule-owner-selected comparison behavior, and
  any approved allowlist.
- **Intended output:** A versioned draft review report containing candidate
  locations, triage reasons, probe results, coverage, unchecked rules, and
  items requiring a human decision.
- **Baseline evidence:** Issue #249 shows what an open investigation can
  contribute. The manually reviewed source inventory and tie probe below
  provide the answer key, not measured workflow performance.
- **Value hypothesis:** A stable minimum check plus an exploratory pass will
  reduce repeated manual search. Moving the controlled rule, fixed checks, and
  report structure into separate resources should make evidence and coverage
  more reproducible than the one-file baseline.
- **Agent contribution:** Run the fixed checks when an implementation exists,
  search beyond the catalog for unexpected paths, read surrounding code,
  explain evidence, and draft output. Label fixed and exploratory results
  separately.
- **Human decision:** The rule owner approves the procedure and classifies each
  result as a defect, documented convention, accepted exception, or not
  applicable.
- **Success measures:** Select the skill for applicable requests and not for
  unrelated requests; find every deliberately noncompliant test call; flag no
  compliant test example; attach rule-specific probe evidence to every finding;
  state what was not checked; and distinguish catalog results from exploratory
  findings. Under an identical environment, the resource-backed version must
  preserve its fixed scan output, probe output, and required report fields
  across repeated runs.
- **Main risks:** A narrow search can produce a convincing false clean report,
  and a polished skill description can create confidence before the underlying
  checks have been implemented and benchmarked.

The Plan gate is the rule owner's decision that a repeatable check is worth
building. The accepted workflow brief initiates Design.

## Design --- Specify the workflow

### Carry the rule and its scope clause forward unchanged

BR-001, BR-002, and BR-003, stated in @sec-workflow-rounding-prompt, are separate
business rules. BR-001 requires exact decimal ties to round half away from zero
and prohibits a displayed negative zero. BR-002 requires calculations to use
unrounded values and to round once for display. BR-003 requires display
precision to be specified and preserved. Each rule is version 1.0 in this
example.

The scope clause attached to BR-001 defines which calls are in scope: any call
that can change a numeric value displayed in a report or used to decide which
rows the report includes. It therefore places `formatC()`, `sprintf()`, and
`format()` among the candidates.

This workflow checks only **BR-001**. BR-002 and BR-003 remain explicit gaps,
declared in every run rather than left unmentioned. For this exercise, the
illustrative rule owner selects the documented behavior of
[`cards::round5()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/CRAN/web/packages/cards/refman/cards.html#round5)
as the comparison behavior. A future implementation must pin the package
version and test the selected behavior, including values near a tie. This is
not an industry endorsement.

### Design two increments of the same skill

The [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification) requires
only a directory containing `SKILL.md`. Its header contains `name` and
`description`, and the name must match the directory name. Directories such as
`references/`, `scripts/`, and `assets/` are optional. That makes it possible to
start with one file and add structure only when the workflow needs it.

This chapter uses two build examples rather than treating the complete folder
layout as the starting point:

| Build example | Contents | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| **1. One-file skill** | `SKILL.md` only | Can one inspectable instruction make the rule, trigger, procedure, boundaries, and output visible? |
| **2. Resource-backed skill** | `SKILL.md` plus `references/`, `scripts/`, and `assets/` | Which limitations require controlled context, fixed execution, or a stable report form? |

Both examples describe the same workflow and use the same skill name. The
second is an evolution of the first, not a separate workflow or a second turn
through the lifecycle. The task contract defines the behavior that both
versions must attempt to provide and identifies where the one-file version is
not strong enough.

### Canonical artifact: Task contract

- **Objective:** Report candidate divergences from BR-001 in one named R source
  folder.
- **Trigger:** An approved on-demand request; automated triggers remain future
  options.
- **Required context:** Target commit, source folder, BR-001 v1.0, the
  function catalog, the selected comparison function and its version, required
  display precision, and any approved allowlist.
- **Fixed, repeatable checks (deterministic work):** Scan a catalog of possible
  rounding and numeric-to-text functions, then probe each provisionally
  in-scope numeric call with decimal ties of both signs at its required
  precision and with negative values that should display as zero.
- **Agent work:** Search beyond the catalog for wrappers and other unexpected
  paths, provisionally determine whether each candidate affects a displayed
  numeric value or a report decision, explain any divergence, and draft the
  report.
- **Required output:** `file:line`, source expression, probe result, supported
  explanation or unresolved cause, discovery method, triage reason, coverage,
  execution environment, and unchecked rules. Results from the catalog scan
  and exploratory search remain labeled separately.
- **Boundaries:** Read and test only; no source edits, policy changes,
  classification approval, or external posting.
- **Stop conditions:** Missing rule version, unreadable files, unresolved
  display precision or tie intent, a documented conflicting convention, or
  failed checks.
- **Human decision:** The rule owner confirms triage, classifies each finding,
  approves exceptions, and authorizes any communication.

The contract describes the target behavior. The one-file example can require
the scan and probe, but it cannot make their execution deterministic by itself.
The resource-backed example assigns that fixed work to separately testable
scripts while leaving exploration and triage with the agent.

The Design gate is approval of the rule scope, task contract, two-increment
build plan, and stop conditions by the rule owner and an R programmer.
Acceptance authorizes a prototype, not a finding or a code change, and
initiates Build.

## Build --- Prototype the workflow

The Build stage makes the proposed skill visible in two increments. These are
manuscript listings, not files distributed by the book. They show how a team
could start with one inspectable instruction and then add resources in response
to evidence about its limitations.

### Example 1: Start with `SKILL.md` only

The smallest conforming skill is one directory containing one `SKILL.md`:

```text
rounding-rule-review/
  SKILL.md
```

The following proposed file makes the trigger, rule, procedure, output, and
stop conditions visible together:

````markdown
---
name: rounding-rule-review
description: Reviews a bounded R source tree for BR-001. Use when a
  reviewer needs call locations, tie probes, coverage, and draft
  findings for human review.
---

# Rounding rule review

## Required inputs

- A pinned source commit and one R source folder
- BR-001 v1.0 and the required precision for each relevant output
- The selected comparison behavior and its version
- Any rule-owner-approved allowlist

## Rule and scope

Apply BR-001: values intended as exact decimal ties round half away from zero,
and a displayed value is never a negative zero.

Include any call that can change a numeric value displayed in a report or used
to decide which rows the report includes. Formatting calls are candidates.

## Procedure

1. List every `.R` file in scope.
2. Search for `round()`, `signif()`, `formatC()`, `sprintf()`, `format()`,
   `prettyNum()`, and `as.character()`.
3. Search beyond that catalog for wrappers and unexpected rounding paths.
4. Read each candidate in context and record whether it can affect a displayed
   numeric value or a report decision.
5. Probe each provisionally in-scope call at its required precision with
   positive and negative decimal ties. For display calls, also test negative
   values that should display as zero.
6. Keep catalog results, exploratory candidates, probe output, provisional
   triage, and human classification separate.

## Required report

Record `file:line`, source expression, discovery method, triage reason, probe
result, supported explanation or unresolved cause, files examined, exclusions,
execution environment, unchecked rules, and items requiring human review.

## Stop and escalate

Stop when the rule version, required precision, tie intent, source, or
comparison behavior is unresolved, or when a check fails. Do not edit source,
change policy, approve a classification, or post an external issue.
````

This one-file version is useful. A reviewer can inspect the whole instruction,
the agent can discover it from its description, and a rule owner can review a
single change. It is also only an advisory procedure. The agent still chooses
how to perform the catalog search and tie probes, the rule is coupled to the
operating instructions, and prose alone does not ensure that every run produces
the same coverage record or output structure.

Those limits are evidence for the next build increment. They are not reasons to
skip the one-file version: a small, low-risk task may not justify more machinery.

### Example 2: Add resources to improve behavior

For this review, the task contract requires stronger separation of policy,
fixed evidence, and presentation. The second example keeps `SKILL.md` as the
entry point and adds only the resources needed for those requirements:

```text
rounding-rule-review/
  SKILL.md
  references/
    br-001.md
  scripts/
    scan-rounding-calls.R
    probe-tie-behavior.R
  assets/
    review-report-template.md
```

The revised `SKILL.md` becomes shorter because it orchestrates the resources
instead of carrying all their detail:

````markdown
---
name: rounding-rule-review
description: Reviews a bounded R source tree for BR-001. Use when a
  reviewer needs call locations, tie probes, coverage, and draft
  findings for human review.
---

# Rounding rule review

1. Read [`references/br-001.md`](references/br-001.md). Confirm its version,
   scope, rule owner, selected comparison behavior, and approved allowlist.
2. Run `scripts/scan-rounding-calls.R` on the approved R source folder. Preserve
   the complete file inventory and catalog candidates.
3. Search beyond the catalog for wrappers and unexpected paths. Label these
   candidates as exploratory.
4. Read every candidate in context. Record provisional triage without silently
   removing excluded candidates from coverage.
5. For each provisionally in-scope call, run
   `scripts/probe-tie-behavior.R` at the required precision.
6. Complete the
   [`assets/review-report-template.md`](assets/review-report-template.md).
   Keep fixed output, exploratory work, agent judgment, and human classification
   separate.
7. Stop before source changes, policy changes, classification approval, or any
   external posting.

If required context is missing or a script fails, record the problem and stop.
````

Each added resource has one job and one intended effect:

| Component | Contents | Behavior it is intended to improve | What it cannot decide |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SKILL.md` | Trigger, sequence, boundaries, and escalation | Consistent activation and orchestration | Whether a candidate is a confirmed defect |
| `references/br-001.md` | Rule text, scope, version, owner, comparison behavior, and allowlist | Traceability to controlled institutional knowledge | Whether the policy should change |
| `scripts/scan-rounding-calls.R` | File inventory and required function catalog | Repeatable minimum coverage | Every dynamically constructed or uncataloged path |
| `scripts/probe-tie-behavior.R` | Fixed inputs, comparison results, and environment capture | Reproducible numeric evidence | Whether a source value was intended as an exact decimal tie |
| `assets/review-report-template.md` | Required fields and separate evidence sections | More consistent, reviewable output | Whether an explanation or classification is correct |

This layout uses progressive disclosure. The agent sees the `name` and
`description` when selecting a skill, loads the `SKILL.md` instructions when the
skill applies, and reads or runs the other resources only when directed. Moving
details out of `SKILL.md` therefore improves separation without hiding the path
the agent must follow.

### How the resource-backed version performs the check

The proposed scanner covers direct calculation functions such as `round()` and
`signif()`, formatting functions such as `formatC()`, `sprintf()`, `format()`,
and `prettyNum()`, and conversions such as `as.character()`. It produces
candidates, not findings. The agent then explores beyond the catalog, reads each
candidate in context, and provisionally determines whether it can affect a
displayed numeric value or a report decision.

The probe runs only for provisionally in-scope numeric calls. It tests positive
and negative decimal ties at the precision required by each call and, for
display calls, negative values that should display as zero. It places the
observed result beside the selected result and reports `PASS` or `FAIL`. If the
required precision or intended tie cannot be determined, the workflow records
the unresolved context and stops.

::: {.callout-note title="Optional technical detail: Comparison call"}
The proposed probe obtains the selected comparison result with this call.
Readers do not need to follow its syntax to understand the comparison.

```r
approved <- cards::round5(x, digits = required_digits)
```

This call is a benchmark comparison for the exercise, not a proposed fix for
`metalite.ae`. A future implementation must record the `cards` version, test
values near a tie, and document how it decides that an input is intended as an
exact decimal tie.
:::

### Preserve the decisions that made the check useful

The written procedure must preserve three decisions:

1. Use the function catalog as a minimum check, then search beyond it for
   wrappers and unexpected code paths. Record whether each candidate came from
   the catalog or the exploratory pass, and classify whether it affects display
   or a report decision.
2. Probe both direct rounding and formatting behavior at the precision used by
   each provisionally in-scope call, including negative values that should
   display as zero. Record the R version, and explain tie mode and binary
   representation as distinct causes.
3. Write findings to a draft and stop before any source change or posting a
   GitHub issue.

It must also state these limits:

- A scanner can miss calls that are constructed only while the program runs.
- An exploratory pass can find patterns outside the catalog, but it cannot prove
  complete coverage.
- If the number of decimal places cannot be determined, the review stops.
- An approved helper remains a candidate until the rule owner approves an
  allowlist entry with a reason and source version.
- Only BR-001 is checked; BR-002 and BR-003 remain gaps.

::: {.callout-warning title="When not to use this skill"}
Do not use this design for nonnumeric reports or for reviews of rounding stage
and display precision, which require BR-002 and BR-003. For a genuinely one-off
review, the rule owner may decide that the exploratory prompt in
@sec-workflow-rounding-prompt is proportionate.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Go further: Review all three rounding rules"}
The two build examples in this chapter remain intentionally bounded to BR-001.
The proposed benchmark in
[`RConsortium/pharma-skills` issue #208](https://github.com/RConsortium/pharma-skills/issues/208)
extends the review to all three rules. It asks a future skill to trace relevant
operations from R package report entry points, execute reproducible witnesses,
and report separate verdicts for tie method, rounding stage, and display
precision.

The broader [`Pharma Skills`](https://github.com/RConsortium/pharma-skills)
repository is an open, community-contributed catalog for pharmaceutical R&D.
Readers can inspect its skill packages, benchmark proposals, and
[Agent Skill Development Lifecycle](https://github.com/RConsortium/pharma-skills/blob/main/LIFECYCLE.md)
to see how agent skills can support AI-first work on open source R packages. The
repository's skills remain drafting aids that require independent review under
the user's own quality process.
:::

### Try the intended behavior without installing the skill

The book does not provide either skill version to Arena.ai. This exercise sends
the intended behavior as a prompt so that a reader can inspect a fresh response.
It demonstrates why the definition of which calls are in scope belongs in the
skill rather than in a reviewer's memory. Send this prompt to
[arena.ai](https://arena.ai/agent):

```text
Review the R source from metalite.ae v0.1.4 at the exact commit below for
BR-001: values intended as exact decimal ties must round half away from zero.
A displayed value must never be a negative zero.

Inspect every file under R/. First, run a required catalog scan for calls to
round(), signif(), sprintf(), formatC(), format(), prettyNum(), and
as.character(). Report every catalog match, including matches later excluded
from scope, and label these required-scan results separately from exploratory
candidates.

Include any function call that can change a numeric value displayed in a report
or used to decide which rows the report includes. Formatting functions can
round as a side effect of display. After the catalog scan, choose how to
investigate beyond those named functions, including wrappers or other
unexpected paths, and label those exploratory candidates.

Test decimal ties of both signs at the precision used by each in-scope call. For
display calls, also test negative values that should display as zero. For each
call, report its file and line, observed results, discovery method, R version,
coverage, and unchecked rules. Explain tie mode and binary representation
separately.

Draft a GitHub issue if evidence diverges from the rule, but do not post it. Do
not modify the repository or propose a code change.

Release: v0.1.4
Pinned commit:
https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/tree/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b
```

Arena.ai cannot create the GitHub issue. This is a behavioral preview, not a run
of either proposed skill. Responses vary between runs, so compare the response
with the pinned evidence below rather than expecting a particular answer.

### Canonical artifact: Prototype

No executable prototype artifact exists. At design-pattern maturity, the two
listings specify a one-file baseline and a resource-backed candidate. The
second adds a controlled rule reference, fixed scan and probe interfaces, and a
review-report template; it does not establish that behavior improved.

The Build gate remains open until an R programmer and the rule owner review a
working version of both examples and confirm that the resource-backed candidate
exposes fixed results separately from agent judgment. Only their acceptance
would initiate a comparative benchmark against synthetic cases and the pinned
source.

## Test --- Benchmark and evaluate

The benchmark must evaluate two different failure modes. First, does the agent
select the skill for an applicable request and leave it unused for an unrelated
request? Second, after selection, does the skill produce the required evidence
and coverage? Adding files counts as improvement only if the second example
performs better against predefined criteria.

### Test whether the skill is selected

Both examples use the same `name` and `description`, so they should have the
same selection behavior. A future implementation would present differently
worded requests without naming the skill and record whether it loads:

| Request | Expected selection behavior |
|---|---|
| Review a pinned R source folder for BR-001 | Select the skill |
| Find rounding and numeric-formatting calls that can affect an R report | Select the skill and confirm that BR-001 is the governing rule |
| Explain why R and SAS differ at 2.5 | Do not select the repository-review skill |
| Review when rounding occurs under BR-002 | Do not select this BR-001 skill; use a workflow that explicitly covers BR-002 |
| Review text padding in a nonnumeric report | Do not select the skill |

Selection is necessary but not sufficient. A skill can load reliably and still
miss files, probe the wrong precision, or mix evidence with judgment. Those
behaviors require task-level cases.

### Compare behavior with small test examples

A future benchmark would run the one-file baseline and the resource-backed
candidate against the same five small synthetic R programs, with expected
results recorded before either version runs. The cases include a compliant
program, one `formatC()` display call that violates the tie and negative-zero
clauses, one `round()` call before a threshold comparison, one approved-helper
use, and one violation hidden behind a wrapper that is not named in the catalog.
Together they test correct findings, false findings, allowlist handling, and the
exploratory pass.

The book does not distribute these programs, so their outcomes are acceptance
criteria rather than measured skill performance. They also show the cost of a
broad search: it reduces the risk of a false clean report, but the workflow must
retain and explain candidates that do not become findings.

The comparison records detection, false findings, missed problems, file and
candidate coverage, required-field completion, repeated-run agreement, review
time, and stopped runs. The resource-backed version is better only if it
preserves the required findings while making the catalog scan, probe output,
coverage record, and report structure more reproducible. Exploratory paths may
still vary between runs and remain labeled separately.

### Pinned source evidence for the answer key

All `metalite.ae` locations and results below refer to
[`v0.1.4`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/releases/tag/v0.1.4), released
2026-09-01 and pinned to commit
[`bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/tree/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b).
The file count, candidate count, quoted locations, and probe results were
manually reverified at this commit. They define reference evidence for a future
benchmark; they are not output from the proposed skill. Every count, location,
and result must be reverified again before use with another version or commit.

The evidence narrows in three steps:

1. A search for `round(` found one match, where a rounded percentage controls
   whether an adverse-event row passes a reporting threshold.
2. A catalog scan for seven function names found 21 candidate calls: one
   `round()`, eight `formatC()`, one `sprintf()`, and 11 `as.character()` calls.
3. Context review excluded 13 calls that operate on character or structural
   values, leaving eight in-scope calls: one report-filtering decision and seven
   calls that format values for display.

::: {.callout-note title="Why issue #249 is not the answer key"}
[Issue #249](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/issues/249) is a useful
exploratory report, but its location list still requires context review. It
includes [`R/fmt.R:37`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b/R/fmt.R#L37),
where `formatC()` receives character text assembled after the numeric formatting
at line 33. For character input, the
[`formatC()` documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/formatc.html)
describes padding rather than numeric rounding. The issue also cites
[`R/format_ae_exp_adj.R:203`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b/R/format_ae_exp_adj.R#L203),
which is not a formatting call; the direct `formatC()` call is at
[`R/format_ae_exp_adj.R:208`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b/R/format_ae_exp_adj.R#L208).

This difference illustrates why an agent's candidate locations must be checked
before they are counted as findings. The issue title, causal explanation, and
proposed solution also remain proposals for human review. They are not evidence
that BR-001 governs `metalite.ae` or that the proposed code would pass the
benchmark below.
:::

Those manually verified counts define the expected coverage of the required
catalog scan. They do not prove that no relevant wrapper or unexpected code
path exists. A future implementation must report the exploratory pass
separately and test that pass with a seeded example that is not named in the
catalog.

The in-scope calls show where the illustrative rule could affect an
adverse-event report:

| In-scope call | Role in the adverse-event report |
|---|---|
| [`R/format_ae_specific.R:330`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b/R/format_ae_specific.R#L330) | Round a percentage before applying the row-inclusion threshold |
| [`R/fmt.R:33`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b/R/fmt.R#L33) | Format percentages and total exposure |
| [`R/fmt.R:75`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b/R/fmt.R#L75) | Format an estimate or mean |
| [`R/fmt.R:79`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b/R/fmt.R#L79) | Format a standard deviation or standard error |
| [`R/fmt.R:99`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b/R/fmt.R#L99) | Format a confidence-interval lower limit |
| [`R/fmt.R:100`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b/R/fmt.R#L100) | Format a confidence-interval upper limit |
| [`R/fmt.R:122`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b/R/fmt.R#L122) | Format a p-value above the display cutoff |
| [`R/format_ae_exp_adj.R:208`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b/R/format_ae_exp_adj.R#L208) | Format an exposure-adjusted event rate |

The excluded `formatC()` call receives text that is already formatted rather
than a numeric value
([`R/fmt.R:37`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b/R/fmt.R#L37)).
The `sprintf()` call builds JavaScript, and the 11 `as.character()` calls do not
apply a specified decimal precision. They remain recorded as reviewed
candidates rather than silently disappearing from the coverage statement.

The source accepts different precision arguments, so a complete implementation
would construct decimal ties at the precision used by each call. The compact
probe below uses one decimal place to compare the two underlying expressions.
It was run with R 4.6.1 on arm64 macOS. `formatC` and `round` are observed
results; `approved` is what BR-001 requires:

```text
expressions:
  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
  round(x, digits = 1)

 input  formatC  round  approved
-76.05    -76.0  -76.0     -76.1
 -3.05     -3.0   -3.0      -3.1
 -2.05     -2.0   -2.0      -2.1
 -1.05     -1.1   -1.0      -1.1
 -0.05     -0.1   -0.0      -0.1
  0.05      0.1    0.0       0.1
  1.05      1.1    1.0       1.1
  2.05      2.0    2.0       2.1
  3.05      3.0    3.0       3.1
 76.05     76.0   76.0      76.1

formatC disagreements: 6 of 10
round disagreements: 10 of 10
```

### Keep the two causes distinct

The probe uses one-decimal ties rather than the simpler zero-decimal ties of
@sec-workflow-rounding-prompt for a reason: at one decimal place, two separate causes
are visible, and only one of them can be predicted from reading the source. The
divergence is not explained by one blanket claim about "banker's rounding." One
cause determines the direction at a true tie; the other places the stored number
slightly above or below the intended tie:

1. **Tie mode.** The [Base R documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/Round.html)
   describes `round()` as using round-to-nearest-even at a true tie. When a tie
   is exactly representable in binary, such as 2.5 at zero decimals, both
   tested expressions return 2 rather than the rule's 3.
2. **Binary representation.** Most one-decimal ties are not stored exactly.
   For example, 2.05 is stored just below the intended tie, so formatting the
   stored value produces 2.0. Other inputs can fall on the other side of the
   intended tie.

These causes interact, so source inspection alone cannot predict every
direction. That is why the probe, not the reviewer's reasoning, is the evidence.
The probe also exposes the negative-zero risk: formatting the one-decimal result
of `round(-0.05, 1)` produces `-0.0`. At zero decimals,
`formatC(-0.5, digits = 0, format = "f")` produces `-0`. Both violate the
negative-zero clause.

### What both proposed implementations must reproduce

No skill has been run. The results above are the answer key for a future test.
The benchmark applies the accuracy and boundary criteria below to both build
examples. The resource-backed candidate is eligible for release only if it also
preserves fixed outputs and required report fields across repeated runs.

| Acceptance criterion | Required result |
|---|---|
| Applicable selection requests | Select the skill for 2 of 2 requests |
| Out-of-scope selection requests | Do not apply the BR-001 procedure to 3 of 3 requests |
| Test example with one deliberate `formatC()` display call | Detect its tie and negative-zero divergences |
| Test example with one deliberate `round()` filtering violation | Detect 1 of 1 violation |
| Compliant test example | Report 0 false findings |
| Approved-helper test example | Record the reviewed candidate and report 0 findings |
| Test example hidden behind an uncataloged wrapper | Detect it during the exploratory pass |
| `metalite.ae` v0.1.4 at its pinned commit | Reproduce 1 in-scope `round()` and 7 in-scope `formatC()` calls |
| Pinned one-decimal tie probe | Under R 4.6.1 on arm64 macOS, reproduce 10 `round()` and 6 `formatC()` divergences in 10 inputs |
| Coverage | Name 27 files examined, any exclusions, 21 candidates, rule version, and R version |
| Known gaps | State that BR-002 and BR-003 are unchecked |
| Required report fields | Populate every field or state why the run stopped |
| Reproducibility | A reviewer unfamiliar with this chapter obtains the same answer key; fixed scan and probe outputs agree across identical resource-backed runs |

### Canonical artifact: Benchmark report

No benchmark report exists because no prototype has been implemented or run. At
design-pattern maturity, this artifact is specified rather than populated. The
manually verified source inventory and tie probe above form the reference
answer key; they are not workflow performance results.

A future benchmark report must:

- identify both skill versions, the target, workflow components, R environment,
  rule, comparison function, and their versions;
- report skill-selection results for the five activation requests;
- report results for all five synthetic cases and the pinned-source criteria;
- record detected and missed problems, incorrect findings, stopped runs,
  coverage, reproducibility, review time, and triage agreement;
- preserve fixed check output separately from agent exploration and judgment;
- compare each version with the independently maintained answer key and with
  the other version; and
- record limitations and the reviewers' disposition.

The Test gate remains open. It requires the rule owner and an independent
reviewer to accept an executed benchmark report; the person who wrote the
procedure should not be the only person judging whether it works. Only that
accepted report would initiate Deploy.

## Deploy --- Operationalize the workflow

::: {.callout-important title="Design, not implementation"}
The triggers below are options for the owning team. No skill, CI workflow, or
scheduled job has been committed or run.
:::

The Deploy design connects a future accepted prototype to an advisory review
process. It prepares a review record and stops before any external action unless
a named human authorizes it. [Issue
#249](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/issues/249) was posted manually from
one response to the exploratory prompt in @sec-workflow-rounding-prompt. That action
occurred outside the workflow designed here. The public issue is not evidence
that the skill was released, that BR-001 is a `metalite.ae` rule, or that the
package maintainers confirmed the finding.

The team has three trigger options:

- **On demand:** A reviewer requests the check. Setup is minimal, but the
  process still depends on someone remembering to ask.
- **On a proposed source-code change:** The check runs when relevant reporting
  source changes. This is timely but requires rules that limit when it runs and
  control unnecessary findings.
- **Scheduled:** The check runs before a release or after source changes. It can
  detect drift from approved behavior, but the finding may be separated from the
  change that caused it.

The one-file version is the teaching baseline, not the proposed release
candidate. If the comparative benchmark is accepted, the resource-backed
version is the candidate because its rule, fixed evidence, and report structure
can be reviewed and versioned separately. A team could first place it in the
repository-level skill location supported by its agent platform.
Organization-wide distribution would require a separately approved owner,
support model, and change process. This chapter specifies neither installation
path.

The proposed first release is on demand and advisory. Pull-request or scheduled
execution requires separate approval after benchmark evidence shows acceptable
coverage and review burden. A schedule should not rerun unchanged source. The
continuous, change-triggered check is a possible later destination, not the
first release.

### Canonical artifact: Release record

- **Status:** Not released; this is the record structure required before use.
- **Candidate:** The resource-backed version; the one-file version remains the
  benchmark baseline.
- **Release model:** Manual and advisory; a reviewer requests one run.
- **Proposed versions:** `rounding-rule-review` v1.0 and BR-001 v1.0.
- **Scope:** One identified R source folder and commit per run.
- **Permissions:** Read source, run approved local scripts, and write a draft
  report; no network writes.
- **Output:** Versioned draft review report containing findings, probes,
  coverage, execution environment, limitations, run log, and an optional draft
  issue body.
- **Accountable human:** The named rule owner approves release, classifications,
  exceptions, and any external communication.
- **Reversal:** If released, disable the approved trigger and retain the run
  record. A normal advisory run changes no source or external system.

Because it was copied from an exploratory response outside this workflow,
issue #249 is not the Deploy artifact or evidence that the Deploy gate passed.
That gate is explicit rule-owner approval of the release record and any external
communication. An accepted benchmark plus that approval would activate the
chosen trigger and initiate Maintain. Neither event has occurred in this book.

## Maintain --- Monitor and improve

### Make improvement a governed change

An operating check could suggest catalog additions, allowlist entries, triage
patterns, or rule clarifications. Those are proposals. Before a change becomes
active, the rule owner approves changes to `references/br-001.md`, an R
programmer reviews script changes, and an independent reviewer adds or updates
a test example. The workflow owner reviews changes to the trigger, instructions,
and report template. The agent does not edit the rule against which it is
evaluated.

The first list of improvements follows directly from known limitations:

1. Add a rule-owner-approved allowlist for compliant wrappers.
2. Record target commit, versions, files scanned, exclusions, probe output,
   triage reasons, and classifications in a run log.
3. Report files or expressions the check could not evaluate.
4. Keep this BR-001 skill bounded. Develop the comprehensive three-rule scope
   explicitly through the benchmark and review process tracked in
   [`RConsortium/pharma-skills` issue #208](https://github.com/RConsortium/pharma-skills/issues/208)
   rather than silently expanding the active rule.

### Canonical artifact: Monitoring report

There is no operating history because the book distributes no workflow. The
monitoring report is therefore specified, not populated. A future report must
show applicable requests that did and did not select the skill, unrelated
requests that selected it incorrectly, runs by trigger, coverage, confirmed
findings, false positives, missed defects, stopped runs, triage effort, and
unresolved precision. It also records how long an approved BR-001 change takes
to reach the skill and its tests, whether the active skill still names the
current rule version, incidents, and approved changes.

The rule owner reviews that report and chooses among continued use, correction,
retirement, or a new planning cycle. An accepted policy change, incident, or
measured coverage gap is the event that starts the next cycle.

## Summary

@sec-workflow-rounding-prompt showed that a written rule and one open prompt can
produce useful candidates, examples, explanations, and a proposed solution. It
did not treat that response as an answer key. The separate source review in
this chapter identifies one `round()` call used in a report-filtering decision
and seven in-scope numeric `formatC()` calls. Its one-decimal probe diverges from
BR-001 in 10 of 10 `round()` results and 6 of 10 `formatC()` results in the
recorded environment. These are differences from the illustrative rule, not a
maintainer-approved defect classification. Tie mode and binary representation
remain separate causes.

The first build example packages the trigger, BR-001, procedure, boundaries,
and output in one `SKILL.md`. That is the minimal visible skill and may be
proportionate for a small, low-risk review. The second example adds a controlled
rule reference, fixed scan and probe interfaces, and a report template. Each
resource addresses a named limitation while the agent continues to explore and
perform provisional triage.

The design does not assume that more files produce better behavior. A future
benchmark must compare both versions for skill selection, findings, false
findings, coverage, output completeness, and reproducibility. The
resource-backed version becomes a release candidate only if that evidence is
accepted. An executable prototype, an accepted benchmark report, a release,
and operating evidence remain future work.

Readers who want to continue beyond this bounded design can follow
[`RConsortium/pharma-skills` issue #208](https://github.com/RConsortium/pharma-skills/issues/208).
It is the community workspace for extending the exercise into a comprehensive
rounding skill and benchmark that cover BR-001, BR-002, and BR-003.
